title: How to keep your training video library up to date with your product
summary: How to audit and refresh your training video library after product changes, UI updates, or rebrands, without rebuilding from scratch.
body_markdown:
## Why a training video library goes stale


Training video libraries go stale because product interfaces keep changing after a video is published. Every menu, button, and screenshot becomes part of the rendered frame. When a product team moves a control or renames a navigation item, the video continues showing the old path.


UI changes create the most visible errors. A moved button can make an otherwise accurate walkthrough difficult to follow, especially when the narration tells viewers where to click. Small interface changes can affect dozens of videos when[onboarding lessons](https://www.clueso.io/blog/employee-onboarding-videos-with-examples) and feature tutorials reuse the same navigation paths.


Feature updates create deeper problems because they can change what users must do. A new permission requirement, revised workflow, or removed setting may invalidate several steps. Even when the interface looks similar, the video's instructions can produce the wrong result or omit a new decision.


Rebrands can age an entire training video library at once. New logos, colors, product names, and interface labels remain baked into every frame recorded before the launch. The instructions may still work, but the old visuals can confuse users and make current training look disconnected from the product they see.


Video usually takes more effort to update than text because its components depend on one another. You can replace a sentence or screenshot in a document without touching the surrounding content. In a video, a new screen recording may require updated narration, captions, zooms, cursor timing, and transitions. Translated or dubbed versions multiply that work.


A product change rarely identifies every affected asset on its own. You need a video content audit that connects changed screens and workflows to the videos that contain them, then separates cosmetic age from instructions that could block or mislead a viewer.


## Auditing a video library to find what's outdated


Start the audit with a complete inventory of the training video library. For each video, record its owner, product area, intended audience, publication date, last review date, and location. Add usage data such as views and completion rate when your platform provides it. A shared spreadsheet or content database works well because reviewers can filter videos by product area or release.


Review each asset against five signals.


1. **Compare the recorded interface with the current product.** Check navigation labels, button locations, screenshots, cursor paths, and the sequence of actions. You can often inspect thumbnails and key frames before watching the full video.
2. **Search transcripts for changed features and terminology.** Product release notes provide a useful checklist for renamed features, removed options, and revised workflows. Transcript search can flag affected videos faster than manual viewing.
3. **Check visual and spoken branding.** Look for old logos, colors, product names, taglines, and branded introduction sequences. A rebrand may affect the framing around a tutorial even when the product workflow remains accurate.
4. **Use viewing data as a diagnostic signal.** A sharp drop in completion after a product release may indicate that viewers encounter instructions they cannot follow. Low completion alone does not prove that a video is stale, so compare the timing with product changes and viewer comments.
5. **Connect support requests with specific videos.** Repeated tickets about a step covered in training can reveal missing or outdated guidance. When possible, ask support staff which articles or videos customers viewed before contacting them.


Place every reviewed video into one of three buckets:


- **Keep** videos remain accurate and require no immediate work.
- **Refresh** videos still teach a valid task but contain outdated screens, narration, captions, or branding
- **Retire** videos cover removed features, duplicate newer material, or receive too little use to justify an update.


Prioritize refresh work by combining audience impact, degree of inaccuracy, and update effort. High-traffic onboarding videos and required employee training should come first because outdated steps affect many viewers. Videos linked to frequent support tickets also deserve early attention. Long-tail tutorials can wait unless they contain instructions that cause errors, security problems, or compliance risks.


Finish the video content audit by assigning an owner and target date to every flagged asset. Without ownership, a well-categorized inventory can still become another stale document.


## Refreshing content at scale without starting over


Treat each flagged video as an editing decision before assigning production work. Compare its learning objective and recorded workflow with the current product. A video usually needs a partial fix when the workflow still works. A full re-shoot makes more sense when the product update changes the sequence, outcome, or lesson itself.


Use the smallest fix that restores accuracy.


- Replace the voiceover when terminology or instructions changed but the recorded interface remains accurate.
- Update captions when the spoken guidance is correct but names, labels, or accessibility text need revision. Captions cannot compensate for incorrect visuals.
- Re-record a segment when one screen, button, or interaction changed within an otherwise valid walkthrough.
- Re-shoot the full video when several steps changed or when editing separate segments would create awkward transitions.


Batch similar updates instead of refreshing videos one at a time. For example, group every video affected by a redesigned settings page into one recording session. You can capture the shared screens once, apply the same visual treatment, and use consistent wording across the affected lessons.


Templates reduce decisions during each refresh cycle. Keep reusable title cards, caption styles, voice settings, and export presets for each training series. Store source files with the published asset, and record the product version and last review date. When your platform permits, replace the published file in place so existing links, course assignments, and viewing data remain intact.


A recurring queue keeps maintenance tied to product releases. After each release, add the flagged videos to a scheduled refresh batch and assign each one a fix type. Urgent onboarding content can enter the next production cycle, while low-traffic tutorials can wait for a larger batch.


This workflow maintains assets that already exist.[First-time SOP creation](https://www.clueso.io/blog/create-sop-templates) requires you to define the procedure and build the lesson. Library maintenance starts with an established objective and updates only the parts that no longer match the product.

## Where AI-assisted re-recording cuts refresh time


Manual re-editing takes time because each stale video creates a chain of production tasks. An editor reviews the old lesson, rewrites narration around the updated interface, and captures the new screen flow. The editor then records the voiceover and re-cuts the video so the audio matches each action. Even a minor interface change can trigger most of that work when the old screen capture and narration no longer match.


AI-assisted re-recording removes several tasks from that chain. You[capture the current product flow](https://www.clueso.io/blog/published-video-in-15-minutes) once, and software generates a revised script based on the recording. The software can then create the voiceover, synchronize it with the screen actions, and update captions without a separate recording session.


[Clueso](https://www.clueso.io/) uses this screen-recording-first workflow to turn a fresh capture into a polished replacement. Its automatic script enhancement helps preserve the lesson’s intent while adapting the narration to the current flow. Its AI voiceovers also let you replace dated narration without bringing back the original speaker or hiring a voice actor. Editors can reuse approved styling and structure instead of rebuilding the asset around a new recording.


AI-assisted re-recording saves the most time when the interface has changed but the lesson still teaches the same task. A moved button, redesigned menu, or updated brand treatment may require new visuals without requiring a new instructional plan. When a product update changes the task itself, a subject-matter expert still needs to revise the teaching sequence and verify the script. AI reduces production work, but it cannot decide whether the old lesson remains accurate.


Human review should cover product terminology, voiceover pronunciation, timing, and any instructions with security or compliance implications. With those checks in place, AI-assisted re-recording turns flagged videos into a manageable refresh queue rather than a series of full editing projects.

## Building a recurring refresh cadence


L&D or customer education should own the training video library and its maintenance calendar. Product managers can supply release notes and preview access, but one content owner should decide when a release requires review and coordinate the work.


Tie reviews to the product release rhythm. Schedule a review after major interface or branding changes, then run a broader quarterly check for smaller updates that accumulated between releases. Set a service target for high-traffic onboarding videos so critical content gets reviewed before launch or within a defined number of days afterward.


Each scheduled review should feed flagged videos into a shared maintenance queue with an owner and deadline. Batch related updates by feature or product area, then use AI-assisted re-recording when the original screen footage no longer matches the product. A tool such as[Clueso](https://www.clueso.io/) can turn the new screen recording into an updated script and voiceover, which reduces the manual production work required for each refresh.


Track overdue updates and the time between a product release and its corresponding content refresh. Those measures show whether your cadence keeps pace with product development and whether you need more production capacity.

## FAQs


**How often should you audit a training video library?**


A sensible audit cadence checks the library quarterly and after any release that changes core workflows or branding. Clueso fits this cadence by letting you re-record flagged workflows without rebuilding each video manually. Regular checks keep high-traffic onboarding content current before outdated instructions generate support requests.


**How can you tell whether a video is outdated without watching it fully?**


Outdated-video screening compares titles, thumbnails, transcripts, captions, and publish dates against recent product changes. Clueso’s generated scripts and captions make feature names and interface labels easier to search. You can identify likely mismatches quickly, then watch only the relevant segments.


**Should you update or replace a stale training video?**


An update preserves a video when its workflow remains accurate, while a replacement covers major changes to the task or structure. Clueso can regenerate a polished video after you capture the revised workflow in a fresh screen recording. A clear threshold prevents you from overediting obsolete material or discarding reusable content.


**How much time can AI re-recording save compared with manual re-editing?**


AI-assisted re-recording generates a new script and voiceover from an updated screen capture instead of requiring separate scripting, narration, and editing passes.[Clueso](https://www.clueso.io/) automates those production steps after you record the corrected workflow. You can often complete a refresh in one recording cycle rather than coordinating several manual handoffs.
